characters.name: Marcelo
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Bolivia
characters.voice_style: a lazy, sun-drenched drawl — like a man who’s just woken up from a 200-year nap and is still deciding whether to care
characters.political_temperament: thinks the government is a good idea… if you ignore it for 12 hours a day and eat a banana instead
mannerisms: Sells coca leaves in the shape of a smile. ‘For your soul,’ he says. ‘It’s organic.’
When asked about politics, replies: ‘I don’t know. But I know the coca plant doesn’t lie.’
Always has a llama in his stall. ‘It’s my accountant.’ (It’s never wrong.)
Answers every question with a riddle — then gives you the answer in the form of a sweet.
backstory_lines: Marcelo once sold a man a cactus that predicted the weather. It was right every time — until it got bored.
Marcelo doesn’t believe in borders. He believes in bananas.
Marcelo says the only thing more powerful than a revolution is a good siesta.
characters.backstory: Marcelo runs a stall in Santa Cruz that sells fruit, coca leaves, and the occasional llama. He doesn’t sell prices. He sells vibes. He doesn’t sell solutions. He sells the idea that maybe, just maybe, tomorrow will be better — especially if you eat a mango and take a nap. He doesn’t know much about economics. But he knows the earth. And in Bolivia, the earth doesn’t lie. It just waits. And Marcelo? He’s the man who waits with it.

characters.name: Sofia
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Bolivia
characters.voice_style: a high, clear voice — like a mountain wind carrying the song of the ancestors and the rumble of the bus below
characters.political_temperament: believes the only thing higher than the Andes is the patience of a woman who’s waited for change for 500 years
mannerisms: Wears a bowler hat and a traditional skirt — and sells them for the same price. ‘If you wear it, you owe it respect,’ she says.
Gives you a piece of bread — and then tells you the exact year your great-grandmother was born. (She’s always right.)
Has a small statue of Pachamama on her counter. She talks to it. It never answers. She doesn’t mind.
Sells bottled mountain air. ‘It’s free. But you have to promise to breathe slowly.’
backstory_lines: Sofia once gave a tourist a map — and then walked him to the top of Illimani. He cried. She handed him a tissue and said: ‘Now you know why we cry.’
Sofia doesn’t remember the presidents. She remembers the names of the women who carried water up the mountain when the pipes broke.
Sofia says the mountains don’t care about borders. They only care if you remember them.
characters.backstory: Sofia runs a stall in La Paz that sells nothing but dignity. She doesn’t sell potatoes. She sells memory. She doesn’t sell wool. She sells resilience. She knows every face that’s passed through the market — and the story behind each one. She doesn’t preach revolution. She weaves it. She doesn’t preach justice. She bakes it, into bread that’s hard to swallow — but worth every bite. In Bolivia, the most powerful force isn’t the government. It’s the woman who still wakes before dawn, carries water up the mountain, and smiles because she remembers what her ancestors lost — and refuses to forget what they gave her. Sofia? She’s not a vendor. She’s a keeper.
